items.followUp: How does mitosis help a cut or wound heal?

rubric.why: Mitosis produces new cells with the same genetic information as the original cell.
rubric.description: States that mitosis produces genetically identical cells.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the new cells as identical to the parent cell.

rubric.why: The new cells replace old, worn-out or damaged body cells.
rubric.description: Explains that the new cells replace body cells.
rubric.how: Award for linking mitosis with replacement or repair of body cells.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells that are genetically identical to the original cell.
These cells replace worn-out or damaged body cells and help repair tissues.

items.followUp: How does mitosis help an organism grow?

rubric.why: A tetrad forms when homologous chromosomes pair during meiosis.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the pairing that forms a tetrad.

rubric.why: The paired chromosomes consist of four chromatids in total.
rubric.description: Identifies the four chromatids in a tetrad.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the tetrad contains four chromatids (two paired chromosomes).

modelAnswer: A tetrad is formed during prophase I of meiosis when two homologous chromosomes pair.
The pair contains four chromatids in total.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when temperature rises above its optimum?

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, and warming generally increases enzyme activity up to an optimum temperature.
rubric.description: States that the rate rises as temperature increases up to an optimum.
rubric.how: Award for describing the rise in photosynthesis rate before the optimum.

rubric.why: Above the optimum, photosynthetic enzymes lose their functional shape and the rate falls.
rubric.description: States that high temperature denatures enzymes and lowers the rate.
rubric.how: Award for the decrease above the optimum, with enzyme denaturation as the cause.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum because the reactions are enzyme-controlled.
Above the optimum, enzymes denature and the rate of photosynthesis decreases.

items.followUp: Where in the cell does the electron transport chain occur, and what does it produce?

rubric.why: Energy is released gradually throughout respiration rather than in one isolated step.
rubric.description: Explains that energy is released in stages during respiration.
rubric.how: Award for rejecting the idea that all energy release occurs in one step.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain is a sequence of carriers; energy from electron transfer is used to make ATP.
rubric.description: Describes the electron transport chain and its role in ATP production.
rubric.how: Award for identifying electron transfer through carriers and/or its use in ATP formation.

modelAnswer: Respiration releases energy gradually in a series of stages, not in just one step.
In the electron transport chain, electrons pass along carriers, and the released energy is used to make ATP.

items.followUp: Which enzymes in biological detergents help remove protein and fat stains?

rubric.why: Enzymes in detergents break down organic material in stains so it can be washed away.
rubric.description: Explains that detergent enzymes break down biological stains.
rubric.how: Award for stating their role in removing organic stains.

rubric.why: Different detergent enzymes act on particular stain substances.
rubric.description: Gives an enzyme and its stain substrate.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example, such as proteases acting on proteins or lipases acting on fats.

modelAnswer: Biological detergents contain enzymes that break down organic substances in stains, helping remove them during washing.
For example, proteases break down protein stains and lipases break down fat stains.

items.followUp: What happens to the reaction rate when all enzyme active sites are occupied?

rubric.why: Saturation means there are no unoccupied active sites available for additional substrate molecules.
rubric.description: Defines saturation as all active sites being occupied by substrate.
rubric.how: Award for stating that all enzyme active sites are filled or occupied.

accept: adding more substrate does not increase rate
rubric.why: Once saturated, the available enzymes are working at their maximum rate; more substrate cannot increase it.
rubric.description: States the consequence of saturation for reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award for noting the rate is at its maximum or does not rise with more substrate.

modelAnswer: Saturation of active sites means that substrate molecules are occupying all the active sites of the enzymes.
The reaction is then at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.

items.followUp: How does the lock-and-key model explain enzyme specificity?

rubric.why: The model explains specificity by the complementary shapes of an enzyme's active site and its substrate.
rubric.description: States that the active site has a shape complementary to its substrate.
rubric.how: Award for explaining the specific fit between enzyme and substrate.

rubric.why: Binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme can be reused.
rubric.description: Describes binding or the outcome of the enzyme-substrate interaction.
rubric.how: Award for describing the fit, complex formation, product release, or reuse of the unchanged enzyme.

modelAnswer: The lock-and-key model states that an enzyme's active site has a specific shape that fits its substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: How does transpiration pull help water move up through xylem?

rubric.why: Water loss from leaves creates tension that pulls water upward through the xylem.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates a pulling force or tension in xylem.
rubric.how: Award for identifying transpiration pull or tension as the upward force.

rubric.why: Cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous as it is pulled upward.
rubric.description: Explains how cohesion helps maintain the water column.
rubric.how: Award for linking cohesion to a continuous water column or its upward movement.

modelAnswer: The cohesion-tension theory states that transpiration from leaves creates tension in the xylem, pulling water upward.
Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water from the roots to the leaves.
